nature-eco-553.title: Peat swamp forests: tropical trees on deep carbon
nature-eco-553.text: In 1997, burning peat and vegetation in Indonesia released up to 2.57 billion tons of carbon, equal to 40% of average yearly global fossil-fuel emissions. The fuel was peat swamp forest. In these tropical moist forests, waterlogged soil stops dead leaves and wood from fully rotting, building a thick layer of acidic peat. They store far more carbon in their soil than forests on mineral soil. About 62% of tropical peatland lies in the Indomalayan realm, mostly Indonesia, and 36% in the Congo Basin. Drainage, logging and fire speed up decay and release that carbon. Protecting them pays well under {{ref:nature-mkt-092}}, earning more emission reductions per hectare, at lower opportunity cost, than saving other forests.

nature-eco-532.title: Four ways an estuary can form
nature-eco-532.text: San Francisco Bay was made by the earth moving, not by the sea rising. Estuaries are classed by how they formed into four types. Drowned river valleys, flooded as sea level rose, are the most common type in temperate climates. Bar-built estuaries are shallow and cut off from the sea by sand spits or barrier islands, and they are common in the tropics. Fjord-type estuaries lie in deep valleys carved by glaciers. Tectonic estuaries, formed by faulting, volcanoes or landslides, are few, and San Francisco Bay is one of them.

nature-eco-533.title: How fresh and salt water mix in an estuary
nature-eco-533.text: Fresh water is lighter than seawater, so in a calm estuary the river can float right over the sea. Estuaries are also classed by how their fresh and salt water mix. In a salt wedge estuary river flow dominates, and fresh water rides over a wedge of denser seawater. Stronger tides stir the layers into partial mixing. When tides dominate, the water column becomes well mixed, with no change in saltiness from top to bottom. In dry climates, where evaporation far exceeds the inflow of fresh water, inverse estuaries form. Some estuaries are intermittent, the final class.

nature-eco-535.title: Estuaries overloaded with nutrients
nature-eco-535.text: An algal bloom can briefly boost fish numbers, then drive them down. Eutrophication of estuaries is nutrient overloading, mostly by nitrogen, that fuels blooms of algae and harms plants, animals and fisheries. Feedbacks during the process cut available silica and raise nitrogen and phosphorus, letting harmful blooms persist. As the algae die and decay, oxygen keeps falling, and fish populations decline. The losses reach the economy through lower fishing sales; the US fishing industry employs 1.7 million people yearly.

nature-eco-534.title: What people have done to estuaries
nature-eco-534.text: Chesapeake Bay's oysters once filtered the whole estuary every three or four days. After years of fishing them too hard, the job takes almost a year. Estuaries are degraded by pollution, taking too many fish, development, dams and diversions. Because they sit at the bottom of rivers, they gather pollutants from far upstream, and long-lived toxins can build up in aquatic life. Fertilizer and waste runoff deplete oxygen and can create dead zones, cutting water quality and fish numbers. Dams and diversions have shrunk some great desert-river estuaries. The Colorado River Delta is now essentially a salt flat.

nature-eco-506.title: The non-living conditions that shape water life
nature-eco-506.text: Dissolved oxygen often decides how much life a body of water holds, and what kind. It is one of the abiotic factors in aquatic ecosystems: the non-living conditions, such as bottom material, depth, nutrients, temperature, salinity and flow, that shape what lives there. Nitrogen and phosphorus levels decide which algae dominate. Too much algae can kill fish as it decays, and in places like the Gulf of Mexico decaying overgrowth creates oxygen-starved dead zones. Changes far upstream matter too. Dams can reduce spring floods and sediment, letting salt water push into coastal wetlands.

nature-eco-503.title: Lake ecosystems: still waters, deep and shallow
nature-eco-503.text: Still waters range from a temporary rainwater pool a few inches deep to Lake Baikal, 1642 m at its deepest. A lake ecosystem is a still-water, or lentic, freshwater ecosystem of a lake or pond, with its living things and its physical and chemical conditions. Lakes are the main example of still-water ecosystems, which also include ponds and wetlands, in contrast with flowing waters. Depth sets ponds and lakes apart. A pond has its whole bottom in light. A lake has a dark deep zone, the profundal. Ponds have an open-water zone and a bottom-and-shore zone, called the benthic zone.

nature-eco-500.title: Marine coastal ecosystems: where land meets ocean
nature-eco-500.text: Earth has about 620,000 kilometres (390,000 mi) of coastline. Along it lie marine coastal ecosystems, the parts of the sea where land meets the ocean. Coastal habitats reach out to the edge of the continental shelves, the shallow underwater margins of the continents, covering about 7 percent of the ocean's surface area. That thin band includes many different habitats and stands out for high biodiversity and productivity.

nature-eco-453.title: Coral reefs: rainforests of the sea
nature-eco-453.text: Coral reefs cover less than 0.1% of the ocean, about half the area of France, yet they house at least 25% of all marine species. A coral reef is an underwater ecosystem built by reef-building corals. Each coral is a colony of tiny animals called polyps, held together by calcium carbonate, the mineral in limestone and shells. Shallow reefs, sometimes called rainforests of the sea, are among Earth's most diverse ecosystems. Over 4,000 species of fish live on them. Reefs are estimated to cover 284,300 km2, 91.9% of it in the Indo-Pacific region. They grow best in warm, shallow, clear, sunny and agitated water, even though that water holds few nutrients. Reefs also protect their neighbours. Fringing reefs, which hug the shore, shield nearby mangroves and beds of underwater sea plants from strong currents and waves. Reefs are both ancient and young. They first appeared 485 million years ago, but most living reefs are less than 10,000 years old. And they are vanishing fast: shallow tropical coral reefs have declined by 50% since 1950.

nature-eco-558.title: Seagrasses: flowering plants that went back to sea
nature-eco-558.text: Per hectare, seagrass beds hold twice as much carbon dioxide as rainforests. Seagrasses are the only group of flowering land plants that grows in the sea, usually forming meadows in shallow, sheltered coastal waters. About 60 fully marine species exist. They evolved from land plants that recolonised the ocean 70 to 100 million years ago, and most pollinate and complete their whole life cycle underwater. Seagrass beds hold more than 10% of the ocean's carbon storage. Seagrass is an ecosystem engineer that reshapes its surroundings. Its roots hold sediment in place and its blades damp waves, reducing erosion of the shore and the storm-driven rise in sea level. They feed turtles, manatees and fish, and serve as nurseries for commercially valued fish, scallops and shrimp. They cover only 0.1–0.2% of the ocean surface, and over 20% of global seagrass area has been lost since the late 19th century, at 1.5% a year. About a quarter of species (15 of 72) could be rated Threatened or Near Threatened on the {{ref:nature-acct-076}}.

nature-eco-428.title: Salt marshes: tidal grasslands of the coast
nature-eco-428.text: Measured as net productivity, salt marshes are matched only by tropical rainforests. A salt marsh is a coastal wetland between land and sea, regularly flooded by tides and covered with dense salt-tolerant herbs, grasses or low shrubs. Marshes form on sheltered, calm shores of temperate and high latitudes, such as estuaries and the back side of barrier islands. In the tropics and subtropics, mangroves take their place, with salt-tolerant trees instead of soft-stemmed plants. A later study conservatively put global saltmarsh area at 90,800 km2, with the largest marshes outside the tropics. Marsh plants trap and bind sediment, which keeps the marsh stable. Salt marshes feed coastal food webs, deliver nutrients to coastal waters, support land animals and protect coasts. They also serve as sheltered feeding and nursery grounds for migratory fish.

nature-eco-456.title: What coral reefs are worth, and why estimates differ
nature-eco-456.text: About 500 million people benefit from coral reef ecosystem services, chiefly tourism, fisheries and protection of coastlines. Putting a price on them has proved hard. The global economic value of coral reefs has been estimated at between US$29.8 billion and $375 billion per year, and other studies give figures far higher. Estimates of the annual global value differ by orders of magnitude, so any single number should be read with caution. Local figures are firmer. A study in Belize valued reef and mangrove services at $395–559 million a year, and Bermuda's reefs were valued at $722 million a year on average. Fish are a big part of it. About six million tons are taken from reefs each year, and a well-managed reef yields on average 15 tons of seafood per square kilometre a year. Southeast Asia's reef fisheries alone yield about $2.4 billion in seafood annually. Losing reef is costly: destroying one square kilometre was estimated to cost between $137,000 and $1,200,000 over 25 years. To help coastal policy, the {{ref:nature-hist-032}} built tools to value reef tourism, shoreline protection and fisheries.

nature-eco-422.title: Kelp forests: underwater woods of brown seaweed
nature-eco-422.text: Kelp forests and coral reefs together cover only 0.1% of Earth's surface, yet they account for 0.9% of global primary productivity. A kelp forest is an underwater area densely grown with kelp, a large brown seaweed; smaller patches are called kelp beds. They are counted among the most productive and dynamic ecosystems on Earth. Kelp forests grow along temperate and polar coasts worldwide, and in 2007 they were also found in tropical waters near Ecuador. Kelp acts as an ecosystem engineer, building the physical habitat for fish, invertebrates, seals, sea otters and seabirds. These forests can shape coastal ocean patterns and provide many ecosystem services. They are also fragile. Taking too many fish, along with climate change, has all but wiped them out in vulnerable places such as Tasmania's east coast and Northern California.

nature-eco-486.title: Seagrass meadows: grassland under the sea
nature-eco-486.text: Seagrass meadows are being destroyed at about 3 square metres per second. A seagrass meadow is an underwater ecosystem made up of seagrasses, flowering plants that grow in shallow coastal and estuary waters. These meadows rank among the most productive ecosystems on Earth, supporting marine life as diverse as coral reefs do. Seagrasses descend from land plants that returned to the sea about 75 to 100 million years ago. They grow on the continental shelves of every continent except Antarctica, down to depths of about 60 metres. They prefer sheltered bays, lagoons and estuaries, where waves are small and light and nutrients plentiful. The meadows shelter endangered species such as seahorses, turtles and dugongs, and they are nurseries for shrimps, scallops and many commercial fish. The threats are pollution from land runoff, dredges and trawls, and taking too many fish.

nature-eco-457.title: Coral reefs as natural breakwaters
nature-eco-457.text: Reefs can cut wave energy by 97%, and many small islands would not exist without them. Coral reefs protect coastlines by absorbing wave energy before it reaches the shore, helping prevent deaths and property damage. They damp waves as well as or better than artificial breakwaters, and in the tropics restoring reefs is much cheaper than building breakwaters. About 197 million people living below 10 m elevation and within 50 km of a reef may get risk reduction from them. The top meter of reef does much of the work. Without it, expected flood damage would double and costs from frequent storms would triple. For 100-year storms, the kind expected about once a century, flood damage would rise by 91% to $US 272 billion.

nature-eco-458.title: What is killing coral reefs
nature-eco-458.text: Coral reefs worldwide declined 14% from 2009 to 2018. They are threatened by nutrient pollution, warming and acidifying oceans, {{ref:nature-res-027}} and destructive uses of land and sea. Some threats are local: coral mining, dragging nets along the seabed, blast fishing, too much fishing and marine pollution, which persist where regulation is weak. Too much fishing and excess nutrients from land let algae outcompete and kill coral. The global threats are larger. Greenhouse gas emissions warm the sea and raise sea level, causing widespread loss of coral cover as stressed corals turn white. Ocean acidification slows the corals' building of their limestone skeletons and speeds its dissolving, though corals can partly adjust. The outlook is stark: 70–90% of today's warm-water coral reefs will disappear even if warming is kept to 1.5 °C.

nature-eco-460.title: Protecting coral reefs: what works
nature-eco-460.text: Healthier Caribbean reefs have large parrotfish populations, found in countries that protect parrotfish and ban fish trapping and spearfishing. Coral reefs are protected mainly through marine reserves, known as {{ref:nature-res-024}}, plus limits on fishing, pollution and coastal development. These reserves aim at responsible management of fishing and habitat protection, and can also serve restoration, biodiversity and economic goals. How well they work is still debated. Some studied sites showed no difference from unprotected areas, and some caused local conflict. Others provide local revenue roughly equal to what people would have earned without controls. The evidence suggests reserves can protect reefs, but only with clear management and enough money. Protecting networks of diverse, healthy reefs also preserves the genetic diversity corals need to adapt to new climates.

nature-eco-430.title: Salt marshes under human pressure
nature-eco-430.text: As of 2002, over half the world's population was estimated to live within 60 km of the coast, putting coastal habitats under heavy pressure. Salt marshes have been hit hard. People long treated them as coastal wastelands to be drained, built on or polluted. Marshes were lost to land reclamation for farming, urban development, salt production and recreation. A 2022 study blamed direct human activity for 22% of saltmarsh loss from 1999 to 2019, while 30% of gains came from deliberate actions such as restoration. Urban development of marshes has slowed since about 1970, as people recognised the services marshes provide. A newer threat comes from the sea itself. Rising seas driven by climate change threaten marshes through erosion and drowning.

nature-eco-433.title: Can salt marshes outrun rising seas
nature-eco-433.text: Mean sea level could rise between 0.6m to 1.1m by 2100. Rising seas threaten to flood and erode salt marshes, but marshes can sometimes build themselves up fast enough to keep pace. The rule is simple. A marsh survives only if its surface rises faster than the sea; otherwise it drowns. Drowning starts from within. Rising water opens pools inside the marsh, and their edges erode until the marsh can break up into open water. Marshes fight back with their plants. The plants slow currents and calm waves so that sediment settles. That sediment helps the plants grow, and bigger plants trap still more, a self-reinforcing loop scientists call a positive bio-geomorphic feedback. Marshes have one more escape route: moving inland. That needs accommodation space, room to retreat, which is often blocked by coastal roads, sea walls and other development. A marsh squeezed between rising water and a fixed wall has nowhere to go.

nature-eco-425.title: What kelp forests give people
nature-eco-425.text: One theory holds that the first people to reach the Americas followed a 'kelp highway' of Pacific kelp forests during the last ice age. Kelp forests have mattered to people for thousands of years, and they still provide food, materials, recreation and other benefits specific to these forests. Modern fisheries for kelp-dwelling species such as lobster and rockfish support local economies. Kelp itself is harvested to feed farmed abalone and to extract alginic acid, used in toothpaste and antacids. Recreation such as scuba diving and kayaking brings two separate benefits: income for the industry and enjoyment for the people who take part.

nature-eco-424.title: Otters, urchins and kelp: a trophic cascade
nature-eco-424.text: In Alaska, the fate of a whole underwater forest hangs on one furry predator. Sea otters there are the keystone species, eating the plant-eating sea urchins and keeping them in check. A kelp forest trophic cascade is what happens when that control breaks. Lose the predators, and urchins multiply and graze away the kelp. When otters are removed, for instance by hunting, urchin numbers soar, kelp is overgrazed, and the species that depend on it are lost. The forest gives way to an 'urchin barren', bare rock covered in urchins. This shift is widespread, and the two conditions are seen as alternative stable states, each able to persist once established. Not every coast is so fragile. In Southern California, several predators, including lobsters and large fish, control urchins, so losing one matters less there than in Alaska. Recovery is possible: kelp can return after big shocks such as urchin disease or large temperature shifts. Control also works from the bottom up. Nutrient-rich water rising from the deep lets kelp grow and feed the grazers and the animals that eat them.

nature-eco-427.title: What threatens kelp forests
nature-eco-427.text: In the 2010s Northern California lost 95% of its kelp ecosystems to marine heatwaves. Kelp forests are threatened mainly by too much fishing, pollution, kelp harvesting, invasive species and climate change. The most pressing threat may be {{ref:nature-res-027}}, because removing predators lets the forest collapse into an urchin barren. Heat is the rising one. The 2022 IPCC report says kelp and other seaweeds are suffering mass die-offs and range shifts from extreme heat in most regions. Pollution such as sewage, industrial chemicals, heavy metals and farm runoff has damaged kelp forests in southern California. Managers often limit kelp harvesting and fishing, but that does not protect the whole ecosystem. Marine reserves cover the wider web of interactions. Restoration in California mainly removes sea urchins, using divers and sea otters.

nature-eco-491.title: Seagrass decline: meadows lost at speed
nature-eco-491.text: Some 30,000 km2 (12,000 sq mi) of seagrass has been lost in recent decades, mostly because of human activity. The pace has quickened, from 0.9% per year before 1940 to 7% per year in 1990. Some damage is physical. Bottom-dragged fishing nets and boat propellers tear meadows apart. Much of it is chemical. Excess nitrogen and phosphorus feed algae that smother seagrass and block its light, starting a feedback loop that can replace seagrass with algae. Heavy fishing can make this worse indirectly, since removing top predators may cut the small grazers that keep algae down. Low-oxygen water starves seagrass roots and can kill meadows, and the decay of the dead plants uses up more oxygen. Warming, sediment and coastal development add to the decline. Some models predict Posidonia oceanica, a Mediterranean seagrass, will be extinct or nearly so by 2050. The main protection tools are cutting nutrient and other pollution, marine reserves, and transplanting.

nature-eco-487.title: What seagrass meadows do for coasts
nature-eco-487.text: Near small Indonesian islands without sewage treatment, harmful bacteria such as Enterococcus were 50 percent lower where seagrass was present. Seagrass meadows give coastal areas cleaner water, oxygen, food and shelter. They improve water quality by locking up heavy metals and other toxins, removing excess nutrients and lowering acidity. They release large amounts of oxygen into the water, and their roots carry oxygen into the sediment for the animals living there. Turtles, parrotfish, surgeonfish and sea urchins eat the grass, while small invertebrates feed on films on the leaves. People once gathered seagrass to fertilize sandy soils and to stuff mattresses. Conserving the meadows supports 16 of the 17 UN {{ref:nature-gov-010}}.

nature-eco-461.title: Coral farming: gardening a reef back to life
nature-eco-461.text: Unprecedented reef die-offs worldwide have turned coral restoration into a growing field. Coral farming, also called {{ref:nature-nbs-049}}, grows coral fragments in nurseries and then replants them on damaged reefs. It relies on corals' natural ability to keep growing from broken pieces that anchor to new surfaces. The method skips the early growth stages, when young corals are most likely to die. Nurseries have become the most widespread and arguably most effective restoration method, largely replacing the transplanting of whole colonies.

nature-eco-455.title: Corals and their algae: a partnership in sunlight
nature-eco-455.text: A coral polyp cannot make food from sunlight, yet reefs grow in sunny water for a reason. The polyps live in partnership with tiny algae, called zooxanthellae, inside their tissues. The algae photosynthesize and feed the polyp with sugars and other compounds such as glucose, glycerol and amino acids. The partnership has a breaking point. Stressed corals expel these colourful algae, a response called bleaching.

nature-eco-459.title: Coral bleaching: when heat breaks the partnership
nature-eco-459.text: One study of the Great Barrier Reef found 50% reef mortality after an extreme heatwave with a 3–4 °C rise. Coral bleaching is the stress response in which corals expel the colourful algae living in their tissues. Corals depend on these single-celled algae, zooxanthellae, which feed them through photosynthesis. Lose them and the coral turns white and starts to starve. Most corals tolerate only a 4–5 °C range in temperature, and rising ocean temperatures may be the biggest threat to reefs. Greenhouse gas emissions are warming the seas and causing widespread bleaching. El Niño events, natural warm spells in the Pacific every 4–7 years, also bleach heat-sensitive reefs, with especially widespread bleaching in 1998 and 2010. Reefs can take decades to recover. Yet they are getting less time. A report, Status of Coral Reefs of the World 2025, found the gap between warming events has shrunk to five or six years in many regions. It used to be about a decade. There is some resilience. Corals hosting certain algal types (Clade A or D) resist heat better than those with Clade C, and some reefs become more resistant after a severe event.
